newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: U.S, Canadian firms join South African oil search.
newsitem.headline: U.S, Canadian firms join South African oil search.

text.p: U.S.-based Phillips Petroleum and PanCanadian Petroleum of Canada signed up on Tuesday to join South Africa's offshore oil search.
The companies will join local firms Energy Africa and Sasol in exploring a 14.5 million acre zone off South Africa's east coast.

"It shows international companies share our firm belief that the South African offshore (area) has the potential of further discoveries, and can be seen as an effective prospect for international investors," Mineral and Energy Affairs Minister Penuell Maduna said at the signing ceremony.

Phillips, which has the biggest share of 40 percent in the venture, is committed to spending at least $8.0 million in the first four years of the contract, which could rise to $20 million if options for two further three-year periods are taken up.
The companies will also contribute $100,000 a year to train South Africans in the upstream energy industry.
South Africa is due to start pumping its first offshare crude from the Oribi field off Mossel Bay this month.
The agreement signed on Tuesday gives the companies oil and gas exploration rights in two blocks off South Africa's KwaZulu -Natal coast.
South Africa's state-owned Soekor exploration group said it had found geological structures "worth further investigation" during seismic testing in the two blocks in the 1970s and 1980s.
Maduna said South Africa was keen to attract more companies to its largely unexplored 100 million acres of offshore prospects.

"The South African government accepts that there is work to be done in making the terms and conditions for offshore leases as investor-friendly as possible, and competitive with those offered elsewhere in the world.
"The government is entirely open to negotiation and discussion," he said, adding foreign operators were expressing growing interest in blocks of the Atlantic west coast.
